01.note: Issur, a convert, had twelve thousand dinars on deposit with Rava. His son, Rav Mari, had been conceived before Issur converted and born after, and was away at a study hall when his father lay dying. Rava reasoned aloud that Rav Mari had no way to get the money: he could not inherit it, a deathbed gift counts like inheritance, the coins were not in his hands to pull, coins cannot be acquired by symbolic exchange, Issur owned no land to attach them to, and a transfer in the presence of all three parties needed Rava himself, who said he would not come if sent for. The text here stops before telling how it turned out.
01.why: The Gemara asks whether a dying man's admission that he owes someone money works like a deathbed gift, and opens this case with 'come and hear' as the proof.

people.name: Issur the convert
people.about: A convert who had deposited twelve thousand dinars with Rava and was on his deathbed.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage holding Issur's money, who reasons that Rav Mari cannot acquire it.

people.name: Rav Mari
people.about: Issur's son, conceived before his father converted and born after; away at a study hall.

terms.meaning: A formal way of transferring ownership in which the buyer hands over an object, often a cloth, to seal the deal. The Sages held that coins cannot be transferred this way.

terms.term: in the presence of all three
terms.meaning: A way of transferring money held by a third party: the owner tells the holder, in front of the recipient, to hold it for the recipient instead. It needs all three people there.

terms.term: gift of a person on his deathbed
terms.meaning: A gift made by someone who expects to die soon. The Sages let it take effect by words alone, without the usual formal acts of acquisition, and treated it like inheritance.

01.flag: The STORY segments stop at Rava's reasoning; the outcome (the document of admission and Rava's anger) is in the AFTER segment.

02.note: The mother of Rav Zutra bar Toviyya wrote her property over to her son, saying she did it because she wanted to marry Rav Zevid. She married him, and he divorced her. She then came before Rav Beivai bar Abaye to get her property back. Rav Beivai ruled against her: she gave the property because she wanted to marry, and she did marry, so the gift stands.
02.why: This opens a string of cases, listed by a memory aid just before it, about gifts of property and when they can be taken back. Right after it Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, attacks Rav Beivai's ruling, saying she had stated her reason and the marriage ended.

people.name: Rav Zutra bar Toviyya
people.about: The son to whom his mother wrote over her property.

people.name: Rav Zevid
people.about: The man she wanted to marry; he married her and then divorced her.

people.name: Rav Beivai bar Abaye
people.about: The judge she came to for her property; he ruled the gift valid.

terms.meaning: A written document transferring ownership. Here a woman about to marry uses one to put her property in her son's name so that her new husband does not get it.

03.note: The mother of Rami bar Hama wrote her property over to him one evening, then wrote it over to his brother, Rav Ukva bar Hama, the next morning. Rami went to Rav Sheshet, who gave him the property; Rav Ukva went to Rav Nahman, who gave it to him. Rav Sheshet challenged Rav Nahman: she has died, so how could she have retracted? Rav Nahman answered with Shmuel's teaching that whenever a dying person could have retracted the gift had he recovered, he can retract it even without recovering.
03.why: This is one of a string of cases about deathbed gifts. It turns on whether a dying woman who gave away everything can change her mind and give it to someone else, which Rav Sheshet presses further right after.

people.name: Rami bar Hama
people.about: The son who received his mother's property in the evening; Rav Sheshet ruled for him.

people.name: Rav Ukva bar Hama
people.about: His brother, who received the same property the next morning; Rav Nahman ruled for him.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: The judge who ruled for Rami and then questioned Rav Nahman's ruling.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who ruled for Rav Ukva, citing Shmuel.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage whose teaching Rav Nahman quotes.

terms.term: gift of a person on his deathbed
terms.meaning: A gift made by someone who expects to die soon. If such a person gives away all his property and then recovers, he can take the gift back.
To take back a gift already given.

04.note: The mother of Rav Amram the Pious had a bundle of promissory notes. As she was dying she said: Let them be for Amram, my son. His brothers went to Rav Nahman and objected that Amram had never pulled the bundle, the formal act that transfers ownership. Rav Nahman told them that the words of a dying person count as if written and handed over.
04.why: One of a string of deathbed-gift cases ruled by Rav Nahman. This one shows that a dying person's spoken words alone transfer even documents, with no formal act of acquisition.

people.name: Rav Amram the Pious
people.about: The son to whom his dying mother left her bundle of promissory notes.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who upheld the gift against the brothers' objection.

terms.meaning: Written records of loans that entitle the holder to collect the debt.
A formal way of taking ownership of movable things: the new owner physically draws the item toward himself.

05.note: The sister of Rav Tovi bar Rav Mattana wrote her property over to Rav Tovi one morning. That evening another brother, Rav Ahadvoi bar Rav Mattana, came to her crying and said people would now say that one brother is a Torah scholar and the other is not. So she wrote the property over to him. Rav Tovi came before Rav Nahman, who quoted Shmuel: whenever a dying person could have retracted the gift had he recovered, he can retract it, and so the property went to Rav Ahadvoi.
05.why: Another case in the string of deathbed gifts, applying the rule Rav Nahman has just stated: a dying person who gave away everything may give it again to someone else.

people.name: Rav Tovi bar Rav Mattana
people.about: The brother who received his sister's property in the morning and lost it.

people.name: Rav Ahadvoi bar Rav Mattana
people.about: Another brother, who cried to his sister and got the property that evening.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge, who ruled for Rav Ahadvoi by quoting Shmuel.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage whose teaching Rav Nahman quotes.

terms.meaning: Someone learned in Jewish law and teaching. Rav Ahadvoi feared people would think his sister favored Rav Tovi for being one.

06.note: The sister of Rav Dimi bar Yosef owned part of an orchard. Each time she fell sick she gave it to him, and each time she recovered she took it back. Once, sick again, she sent for him; he refused to come until she told him to acquire it any way he liked, so he left part of it to her and took the rest with a formal act. When she recovered she took it back and went to Rav Nahman. Rav Dimi would not come to court, and Rav Nahman threatened to strike him with a thorn that does not draw blood. Rav Nahman asked the witnesses what had happened; they said she had cried, 'Woe, that woman is dying!' He ruled that she had given it in expectation of death, so she could retract.
06.why: Rav Dimi relied on the rule that a dying person who keeps back part of his property cannot take the gift back. The story shows Rav Nahman making an exception when the gift was clearly made only because death was expected.

people.name: Rav Dimi bar Yosef
people.about: The brother who received his sister's orchard and tried to make the gift stick.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who summoned Rav Dimi, threatened him, and ruled for the sister.

terms.term: thorn that does not draw blood
terms.meaning: Rav Nahman's threat; the translation explains it as excommunication, a ban that cuts a person off from the community.
Kept back part of the property for the giver. A dying person who gives away only part of his property normally cannot take it back if he recovers.

terms.term: one who issues directives due to death
terms.meaning: A person who gives away property only because he expects to die. Rav Nahman rules that such a gift can be taken back.

07.note: The mother of the sons of Rokhel was sick and said: My brooch, worth twelve hundred dinars, shall be given to my daughter. She died, and the Sages upheld her words. Rav Mesharshiyya raised this incident against Rava, and Rava answered that she had spoken in expectation of her death.
07.why: Rava has just said, in Rav Nahman's name, that a deathbed gift of only part of one's property needs a formal act of acquisition. This incident, a part-gift upheld without one, is raised as an objection to him.

people.name: Rav Mesharshiyya
people.about: The Sage who cites the incident as an objection to Rava.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who answers the objection.

people.name: the mother of the sons of Rokhel
people.about: A sick woman who left her valuable brooch to her daughter.

terms.term: one who issues directives due to death
terms.meaning: A person who gives away property only because he expects to die. Rava says such a gift is a special case.

07.flag: The incident itself is a two-line report quoted as an objection; the rest is legal back-and-forth.

08.note: A man whose deed said his gift was given in life and in death came before Rav Nahman in Neharde'a. Rav Nahman sent him to Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba in Shum Tamya, saying that Neharde'a was Shmuel's town, so how could he rule there like Rav? Later a woman with a deed reading 'during life and in death' came before Rava, who ruled by his own teaching that she could not retract. She kept troubling him. Rava told his scribe, Rav Pappa son of Rav Hanan, to write her a ruling with a phrase meant to show it was a ruse. She saw through it and said: May his ship sink, you are deceiving me. Rava had his clothes dunked in water to fulfill the curse, but his ship sank anyway.
08.why: The Gemara has been debating how to read a deed that says a gift is given 'in life and in death', and whether it can be retracted. These two incidents show Rav Nahman and Rava acting on that dispute.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A judge in Neharde'a who would not rule against Shmuel's view in Shmuel's own town.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba
people.about: The Sage in Shum Tamya to whom Rav Nahman sent the man.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge whose ruling the woman would not accept, and whom she cursed.

people.name: Rav Pappa, son of Rav Hanan
people.about: Rava's scribe, told to write the woman's ruling.

terms.meaning: Neharde'a, where Shmuel taught. Judges there followed his rulings over those of Rav, who held a different view on this kind of deed.

terms.term: hire replacements at their expense, or deceive them
terms.meaning: A phrase from a teaching about workers who quit; Rava had it written into the ruling to signal that the ruling was only a trick to send the woman away.

09.note: In Bnei Brak a man sold some of the property he had inherited from his father and then died. His relatives challenged the sale, saying he had still been a minor when he died. They asked Rabbi Akiva whether the body could be examined. He told them they were not permitted to disgrace him, and that the signs of puberty change after death anyway. Rabbi Yohanan and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish then argue over what the incident shows.
09.why: Rabbi Yohanan says proof in such disputes must come from witnesses, and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish says ratifying the deed is enough. Rabbi Yohanan raises the Bnei Brak incident against him, and they debate who held the property and who was bringing the challenge.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The Sage the family asked; he forbade examining the body.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage who raises the incident as an objection.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
people.about: The Sage who answers Rabbi Yohanan's objection.

terms.meaning: Someone not yet legally adult. A minor's sale of land he inherited is not valid, so the relatives claimed the seller was still one.
A teaching of the early Sages not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law. This incident is quoted from one.
Confirming in court that the signatures on a document are genuine, which makes the document valid evidence.

10.note: In Bnei Brak a man sold some of the property he had inherited from his father and then died. His relatives challenged the sale, saying he had been a minor when he died, and asked Rabbi Akiva whether the body could be examined. He said they were not permitted to disgrace him, and that signs of puberty change after death. Rabbi Zeira uses the incident in a discussion of the age at which a young heir may sell, which leads on to Rabbi Hiyya's practice: when a man without signs of puberty came before him, he would tell them to fatten him if he was thin, or thin him if he was fat.
10.why: The Gemara is asking whether an heir can sell his father's land from age eighteen or only from twenty. Rabbi Zeira argues that examining the body would only make sense under the age-eighteen view, and the Gemara answers him.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The Sage the family asked; he forbade examining the body.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: The Sage who raises the incident as an objection.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage who taught how long a man without signs of puberty counts as a minor, and advised changing his weight.

terms.meaning: Physical signs, such as two pubic hairs, that Jewish law uses to decide when a young person becomes a legal adult.
A man who never develops signs of puberty but shows other signs of this condition; at twenty he is treated as an adult.
The ceremony that frees a childless widow from having to marry her late husband's brother. The underdeveloped man takes no part in it.

10.flag: Only the first part is a story (the Bnei Brak incident); the rest of the STORY segments are legal argument about age and puberty, with Rabbi Hiyya's habitual advice.

11.note: A young man under twenty sold his father's property and the case came before Rava. His relatives told him to eat dates and throw the pits into Rava's house; he did, and Rava ruled the sale invalid. While the ruling was being written, the buyers told him to ask Rava why the scroll of Esther costs a dinar and the Master's short document also costs a dinar. He asked, and Rava ruled the sale valid. When the relatives said the buyers had coached him, Rava replied that since he understands when things are explained to him, he knows what he is doing, and the date pits were just excessive impudence.
11.why: Rava taught that a girl of fourteen who understands business can sell. The Gemara says this ruling of his was not stated outright but inferred from this case.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge who first voided the young man's sale, then upheld it.

people.name: Giddel bar Menashya
people.about: The man whose question to Rava gave the ruling this young man was relying on.

terms.meaning: The long handwritten scroll of the Book of Esther, read on Purim. The young man's question compares its price to the scribe's fee for Rava's short ruling.
A silver coin; here the price of a scroll of Esther and the fee for writing the court document.

12.note: Rabbi Eliezer told the Rabbis about a man from Meron who was in Jerusalem and had a great deal of movable property he wanted to give away. He was told there was no way to do it except by attaching the goods to a transfer of land. So he bought a plot of rocky land near Jerusalem and said: The north part goes to so-and-so, with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels, and the south part to so-and-so, with a hundred sheep and a hundred barrels. He died, and the Sages upheld his words. The Rabbis answered that there was no proof here, since the man from Meron had been healthy.
12.why: Rabbi Elazar holds that even a dying man's gifts need the usual formal acts of transfer. The Rabbis had cited the Rokhel brooch case against him; here the Gemara quotes his own case in reply, and the Rabbis reject it.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage who tells the Rabbis this incident.

people.name: the man of Meron
people.about: A man in Jerusalem who wanted to give away his many movable goods.

terms.meaning: Goods that can be carried or led, like sheep and barrels, as opposed to land.
A legal device: movable goods can be transferred along with a piece of land, so the transfer of the land carries them.
A teaching of the early Sages not included in the Mishna; this exchange is quoted from one.

13.note: A man told another: I am selling you the property of bar Sisin. One field was known as the field of the house of bar Sisin, and the seller said it was not really bar Sisin's property, only called that. The case came before Rav Nahman, who gave the field to the buyer. Rava challenged him: Is this the law? The one who wants to take something from another must bring the proof.
13.why: The Gemara sets this case beside another in which Rav Nahman and Rava seem to take the opposite sides, and asks how each Sage can be consistent with himself.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who gave the disputed field to the buyer.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who objected that the buyer should have had to bring proof.

terms.term: the burden of proof rests upon the claimant
terms.meaning: A basic rule of Jewish civil law: whoever wants to take property from the person holding it must prove his claim.

14.note: A man asked another what he was doing in his house. The other answered that he had bought it from him and had lived in it long enough to establish ownership. The owner said he had been away among distant settlements. The case came before Rav Nahman, who told the occupant to go and prove he had lived there. Rava objected: Is this the law? The one who wants to take something from another must bring the proof.
14.why: The Gemara sets this case against the bar Sisin case just before it, where Rav Nahman and Rava each took the opposite side, and goes on to explain why their rulings do not contradict each other.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who told the occupant to prove his years of residence.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who objected that the claimant should bear the burden of proof.

terms.meaning: A rule that someone who has openly used a property for three years without protest is presumed to own it, even without a deed.

terms.term: the burden of proof rests upon the claimant
terms.meaning: A basic rule: whoever wants to take property from the person holding it must prove his claim.

15.note: A tied document came before Rabbi, and he said there was no date on it. His son, Rabbi Shimon, suggested the date might be hidden between the folds. Rabbi opened it and found the date there, then looked at his son with displeasure. His son said: I did not write it, Rabbi Yehuda Hayyata wrote it. Rabbi told him: Turn away from this malicious speech.
15.why: The discussion has been about tied documents, folded and signed on the back, and how they are written. This incident about one leads straight into a second like it and into a teaching on malicious speech.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi; he found the hidden date and rebuked his son.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi's son, who guessed where the date was and named the writer.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda Hayyata
people.about: The man Rabbi Shimon says wrote the document.

terms.meaning: A document folded over and tied, with witnesses signing on the back between the folds, so that parts of the text, such as the date, are hidden inside.
Saying things about another person that can harm him, even when true. Jewish teaching counts it as a serious sin.

16.note: Another time Rabbi Shimon was sitting before his father, Rabbi, reading a section of Psalms. Rabbi said: How straight this writing is! Rabbi Shimon said: I did not write it, Yehuda Hayyata wrote it. Rabbi told him: Turn away from this malicious speech.
16.why: It follows a similar exchange about a tied document. The Gemara then asks why mere praise counts as malicious speech, and answers that praise of a person can lead others to speak against him.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: Rabbi's son, reading from Psalms.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who praised the writing and rebuked his son.

people.name: Yehuda Hayyata
people.about: The man Rabbi Shimon says wrote the book.

terms.meaning: Saying things about another person that can harm him. The Gemara goes on to say that even praise can lead to it.

17.note: Once in Jerusalem the price of a pair of birds for offerings rose to golden dinars. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel swore by the Temple that he would not go to sleep that night until the price was down to silver dinars. He went into the court and taught that a woman with five definite births or five definite discharges brings one offering and may eat from offerings, and the rest are not required of her. That same day the price fell to a quarter of a silver dinar.
17.why: The Gemara is proving that two plural forms of 'dinar' mean different coins, gold and silver. This incident, from a mishna on women's offerings, shows the two words used for very different prices.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: The Sage who swore to bring the price down and changed the ruling in court.

terms.meaning: Pairs of birds, the offering a woman brought after childbirth or after an irregular discharge of blood.
A woman who has had an irregular discharge of blood from the uterus; she must bring an offering when she becomes pure.
Two plural forms of dinar. The Gemara says the first refers to gold dinars and the second to silver ones, which are worth far less.

18.note: A tax collector came to Abaye and asked to see his signature, so that when rabbis showed him notes signed by Abaye he could let them pass without paying the tax. Abaye signed at the top of the parchment, but the tax collector kept pulling it so the signature would land at the bottom. Abaye said to him: The Sages already anticipated you.
18.why: Abaye has just taught that one should never show one's signature at the bottom of a sheet, since someone could write a debt above it. This incident shows him following his own rule.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage whose signature the tax collector wanted; he signed at the top.

terms.meaning: Treated animal skin used as writing material for documents.

19.note: A bill of sale said the buyer was getting one third of an orchard. The buyer erased the top and bottom of one letter so that it read 'one third, and the orchard', claiming the whole orchard. When it came before Abaye, he asked why there was so much space around that letter. He had the buyer bound, and the buyer admitted it.
19.why: The Gemara is collecting Abaye's warnings and cases about forged documents; just before, he taught where to place numbers so they cannot be altered. This is one of his forgery cases.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The judge who spotted the forgery from the spacing of the letters.

terms.meaning: A written document recording what was sold.
Two Hebrew letters. Turning the wide beit, meaning 'of', into the narrow vav, meaning 'and', changed 'a third of the orchard' into 'a third, and the orchard'.

20.note: A bill of sale gave the buyer the portions of Reuven and Shimon, brothers. They had a third brother named Ahai, a name spelled like the word for 'brothers'. The buyer added one letter so that it read 'Reuven and Shimon and Ahai', claiming the third brother's share too. When it came before Abaye, he asked why the letters were so crowded around that added letter. He had the buyer bound, and the buyer admitted it.
20.why: It is the second in a run of forgery cases brought before Abaye, after his teaching on how to write documents so they cannot be altered.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The judge who spotted the forgery from the crowded letters.

people.name: Reuven
people.about: One of the brothers whose portion was sold.

people.name: Shimon
people.about: One of the brothers whose portion was sold.

people.name: Ahai
people.about: Their brother, whose share the buyer tried to add by forgery.

terms.meaning: A written document recording what was sold.
A narrow Hebrew letter meaning 'and'. Squeezing one in turned 'brothers' into 'and Ahai'.
